revisions.title: A consultation about forming the sons
revisions.body: Lysimachus turns a family embarrassment into a consultation. He and Melesias describe their fathers’ reported noble deeds, while admitting that neither has deeds of his own to recount; their sons also carry ancestral names. The fathers therefore ask what the boys might learn or practice to become excellent, and invite Nicias and Laches to judge fighting in armor as counselors and partners in their care.

revisions.title: Two reasons to accept examination
revisions.body: One way to read this exchange is as a contrast between two reasons for accepting examination. Nicias treats Socratic testing as a useful reminder that can make one more provident and keep one learning. Laches is conditional: he judges a speaker by whether deeds fit words, then says Socrates may have that quality, citing shared danger and a displayed proof of virtue. One way to read the contrast is that Laches' trust remains conditional, not a verdict already secured.

revisions.title: The definition fails, but the inquiry continues
revisions.body: Socrates’ counterexamples make “wise endurance” unstable: Laches is led to judge the less-skilled fighter more courageous, exposing the definition’s contradiction with the earlier rejection of foolish endurance. Yet Laches does not withdraw. He says courage has escaped his words, agrees to persist in the inquiry, and then accepts Socrates’ proposal to bring Nicias into the hunt.

revisions.title: From craft knowledge to the animal reductio
revisions.body: Nicias turns a Socratic maxim into a definition: courage is knowledge of what is terrible and what is encouraging. Laches tests that definition against doctors, farmers, and other craftsmen. Nicias answers by separating craft knowledge from judgment about what is better to suffer or avoid. Socrates then drives the definition toward its animal consequence: either no beast is courageous, or beasts must share courage alike by nature.

revisions.title: From mockery to staged assent
revisions.body: At 197d–198a, Socrates answers Laches’ mockery by shifting attention to Nicias and keeping Laches in the inquiry. He restarts from the premise that courage is one part of virtue, then leads Nicias through a qualified chain: fear concerns expected future evil; the bold concerns future things that are not evils or are goods; and one knowledge spans past, present, and future. The force is the staged accumulation of assent.

revisions.title: From preferred teacher to shared apprenticeship
revisions.body: The decisive turn is not Socrates refusing the assignment. He refuses the premise that anyone has earned priority: the preceding discussion has left everyone equally at a loss, so no one should be chosen over the rest. His answer is collective—seek the best teacher first for themselves, then for the boys. Homer’s quotation removes shame from admitting need, turning apparent demotion into a shared method of learning.
